Students are expected to report on the ground in Latinx neighborhoods in Chicago. This advanced reporting class will provide opportunities for students to dig deeper into systemic inequity in communities of color around the Chicago area, with a focus on social justice issues like education, health and immigration. Students will function in a newsroom setting to submit pitches both pitch and work on stories. Class trips to Latinx neighborhoods will also be central to learning how to work with vulnerable sources.

course_details.Overview of class: Publishers learned long before the algorithmic feed that a good story sells. From fabricated stories of life on the moon in the 1830s to today's "pink slime" news sites, clickbait headlines, and AI "slop," hoaxes and other attention-grabbing content have been built to enrich their creators or extend their influence. This seminar traces the history of the attention economy from the penny press to today's feeds, and it asks how journalism, propaganda, political messaging, and fake news have competed to capture and shape audiences. Each week pairs a foundational theory from the psychology of narrative and media persuasion with a historical or contemporary case, and students bring examples of their own to further test the theory. Along the way, students examine who profits from our attention, how media frames serve to represent events and communities, and how to build media literacy habits (asking for evidence, reading laterally, and following stories over time) that help us engage with information as active participants instead of passive targets of endless "engagement."

course_details.Overview of class:
Stereotypes. Coded language. Unconscious bias. How do these concepts factor into the media search for truth? How might they stand in the way of public understanding of social difference? Clearly, the media affect the way we see one another across social boundaries established by such characteristics as race, ethnicity, gender and sexuality. How do the perspectives formed by this "mediated reality" ultimately affect our decisions on public policy in such areas as political participation, equal rights and criminal justice? These and other considerations are central to professional journalism responsibility and enlightened public choice making. Without question, the media are vital to the effective operation of our democratic system by providing information that should be free of the kind of bias that can distort the public participation process.

Through discussion of principles of media professionalism and ethics, and an examination of some of the hot topics featured in today's headlines, this course will set a framework for recognizing and analyzing media narrative framing, as well as the representation of traditionally marginalized groups within that narrative frame. Ultimately, we will develop a deeper appreciation of media responsibility. Just as important, we will expand our sense of media literacy in considering a path forward—whether as professional journalists or engaged citizens—as we navigate the challenging terrain of an increasingly diverse society and the need for deeper public understanding of this dynamic change in the interest of encouraging meaningful public discourse.

course_details.Overview of class: For generations, investigative reporting has proven to be one of the highest and most impactful forms of journalism. This is a two-quarter class based in Evanston in the winter and Washington, D.C. in the spring. With approval from the instructor, it is possible to be part of the program remotely in the spring. course_details.Overview of class:
This course is a multi-faceted look into an industry that is ever-changing, always challenging but continues to serve an eager and discerning audience. What does exceptional sports reporting and storytelling look like in 2025? We will examine both the industry and the craft; the biggest stories and most compelling issues and we will learn how the best reporters are not coincidentally the best writers.

Sports writing occupies a unique corner of journalism. Though industry layoffs and economic uncertainty has captured plenty of deserved attention in recent years, there is still a growing demand for content. We'll look at areas of tremendous change and that deserve our attention such as college sports, women's pro sports, the multi-billion dollar betting industry as well as the mental health of athletes.

How do we write richly reported and engaging stories that will satisfy and compete for the attention of an audience that has such a vast number and variety of sources and platforms to choose from?

That will be one of our goals this quarter. And to that end, we will hone the fundamentals you first learned in 201-1, work on generating original ideas, crafting stories on deadline and we'll introduce you to sports visualization, all the while being ready to pivot on a daily basis as news and current events occur.

We will talk to top journalists, industry professionals, coaches and others to glean their wisdom and advice. And finally, along with varied in-class assignments, including the NFL Draft and other reporting opportunities, there will be a trip outside the classroom to cover a WNBA game at Wintrust Arena as credentialed reporters on deadline, which I hope will be one of the highlights of a great quarter!

course_details.Overview of class: This course has a professional goal and an academic one. The former is to make you your own best risk counselor in matters of media liability and to prepare you to talk knowledgeably with editors or legal counsel about your work. The latter is to situate those liability risks in the normative, economic and architectural features of the U.S. and international media systems -- in other words, why the system works as it does. The course is rooted in the constitutional, common law, statutory and regulatory systems of media accountability used in the United States as they have developed in the 20th century, and especially since 1964. Since Medill has a campus in Qatar, we consult comparative law examples interpretive of Article 19 of the International Covenant for Civil and Political Rights. We begin the course normatively, by putting all this in the context of First Amendment theory and doctrine. After that it's communications law, and each week we'll consider problems practical and principled, profound and pathetic. Typical topics are incitement, prior restraints, copyrights, defamation, privacy and newsgathering activities. While the course is primarily lecture, on the law school model, I strongly encourage student discussion and to that end we do regular pre-publication review assignments in and out of class.
course_details.Class Materials (Required): There is no text to purchase, though I will recommend an inexpensive casebook as a desk reference. All readings are on Canvas.

course_details.Overview of class: As described in the title of this course, we will take up careful consideration of the legal and ethical issues confronting professional journalists during these challenging times. We begin with a discussion of the kinds of ethical dilemmas we face in our work on a daily basis in such areas as individual privacy interests as set against the public right to know. The point throughout the course is to develop an analytical framework to make determinations under the routine pressures of reporting, editing and publishing in a way that meets our responsibility to the public. A significant amount of our time also be devoted to U.S. media law in the broader context of U.S. Constitutional principles and law. We will learn basic legal vocabulary terms in order to facilitate lively debate and understanding of the material. This section of the course relies on the case study method - reading actual judicial opinions to derive the legal "rule" that governs various media law disputes - in order to allow students to obtain the most realistic picture of the law obtainable by non-lawyers. Students will engage in written and oral argument using major U.S. Supreme Court cases to more fully understand the difficult job appellate judges have in making sound precedent for society that resonates beyond the facts of a particular case. We cover the basic areas of First Amendment law, such as prior restraint, libel, obscenity and time-place-manner restrictions. Throughout both sections of the course, we will employ a light version of the Socratic Method of teaching through inquiry during classroom discussion. We ask questions. We answer the questions. We question the answers. Apart from the ethical and legal principles we will take up, this kind of in-class discourse prepares students effectively for professional journalism success.

course_details.Topic: The Innovative Editor: Human Smarts with AI
course_details.Overview of class:
This 10-week course solidifies essential skills— from story ideation to precision in grammar, style, structure, and clarity—before introducing technology as a collaborative tool for innovative problem-solving. Students will review what makes good writing and editing. Then we will apply generative and agentic AI to see if and how technology can help us enhance stories, develop workflows, and address editorial challenges while preserving journalistic integrity, accuracy, authorial voice, and ethical standards.

This will be a learning lab with hands-on skill development, emphasizing practical editing abilities alongside critical thinking about technology use. We are not trying to master the latest tools or models. We are striving to develop values-based policies and practices and become thoughtful, adaptable editors equipped for the modern newsroom and workplace.

course_details.Overview of class:
As a journalist, you'll often report in communities that are new to you. So how do you come to understand what a neighborhood looks like to the people who live there, what issues matter to them, and how those experiences shape what they expect from the news and what you can offer them? This course teaches you how to answer questions like these, with hands-on instruction and practice in social science methods, like observation, field notes, in-depth interviewing, and analysis, that add to your reporting toolbox.

You'll practice fieldwork skills on campus and in one Chicago neighborhood you return to all quarter, write short vignettes of a place, a person and a practice, and weave them into a final project. Along the way, you'll compare these methods with how you've reported before and work through where they line up with journalism's expectations, where they diverge, and how you might bring them into your own work.

This class is a good fit for students who want to get better at connecting with people, including those who find interviewing intimidating. It covers building trust and rapport within a community, becoming more comfortable in spaces where you're new or an outsider, and letting conversations unfold. You'll also learn to use observation to "read" people and a community, and develop tools to get more out of the "data" you collect. These skills serve any beat and may be of particular interest to students drawn to solutions and community-focused journalism, or interested more broadly in how audiences and communities find and use news. Questions about whether this class is a good fit? Feel free to reach out to Professor Battocchio at afbat@northwestern.edu.

course_details.Overview of class: This quarter, we'll take an up-close look at the fine art of being a general assignment sports reporter, a dive into the professional golf tour and college sports, and how the best sports journalists can cover them all, sometimes at a moment's notice. Even if you came to Medill thinking you'd like to specialize in one sport, there are multiple reasons why leaving yourself open to a variety of assignments will give you a broader perspective and flexibility that will serve you well in your job search. course_details.Overview of class:
This course is the first part of the Medill Investigative Lab-Chicago, where students will work as a team on an in-depth investigative project for publication, over the course of two academic quarters, while also producing their own in-depth investigative story and learning investigative skills applicable to all topics.

The program is based in Chicago and investigations are national, with travel possible. This course combines both undergraduate and graduate students; students will work together with the professor and media partners to report, write and produce stories for publication in professional outlets. This year's lab will focus on reporting on immigration court, as part of a collaboration with other universities nationwide; and students will also do investigations on other aspects of immigration, including mental health care for immigrants.

This winter-quarter course is a mandatory component of the Medill Investigative Lab-Chicago, where we will begin the team investigation that will be completed during the 2-credit spring-quarter course.

In 2022, the Medill Investigative Lab-Chicago worked with Detroit Public TV and Energy News Network to produce a package of investigations about toxic coal ash. In 2023, 2024 and 2025, the Medill investigative Lab-Chicago worked with various local and national media outlets on stories investigating police response to mental health crises, with students traveling to report in locations including Puerto Rico, Atlanta, Rapid City, Charlottesville, Chapel Hill and Minneapolis. In 2025 the lab did a deep dive into policing of mental health crises in Chicago, and the city's alternate response program, with stories published in the Chicago Sun-Times, MindSite News and South Side Weekly.

In 2026, the lab reported on Chicago's immigration court and published a series of stories with Borderless Magazine. In 2027, the lab will again focus on immigration court and immigration-related stories.

While reporting on the focus topic, students will use investigative tools and techniques including FOIAs and public records, court documents, data, mapping, on-the-ground scouting, interviews and other research, developing skills that are transferable to other topics as well.

The program involves a systematic team investigation, wherein students will take ownership of different pieces of the investigation and also produce their own stories ideally for publication as part of the larger project.

Using various documentary TV series as a guide — including Anthony Bourdain's "Parts Unknown" and "Street Food Latin America" and "High on the Hog" on Netflix — we'll explore cinematic journalism, engaged and evocative writing, the finer points of editing and the deeply moving nature of people-centered stories. This will involve weekly readings and viewings, class room discussions, engagement with professionals, exercises with the camera and other assignments designed to help you prepare to create richly visual stories in CDMX. course_details.Overview of class: This course will prepare students to report in a new location - Puerto Rico - on complicated, sensitive and newsworthy topics including environmental justice, climate change, disaster recovery, politics, inequity, food security and public health. Students will explore history, politics, journalism and other context relating to Puerto Rico and Chicago's Puerto Rican diaspora, and learn how to identify and produce timely news or feature stories that build on and recognize this context. Students will find and build relationships with sources from afar and on the ground in Puerto Rico, and experience reporting on critical situations like the aftermath of natural disasters and high-stakes battles over land, as well as contentious politics including the debate over Puerto Rico's political status. During the trip, we will be based in the capitol city of San Juan, and also travel to various parts of the island including the mountainous interior and the south coast, the epicenter of struggles over environmental justice, energy production and food security. Students will work together as a team and also have the opportunity to learn how to arrange their own interviews and logistics during travel reporting. course_details.Overview of class:
This course is an intensive news reporting class focused on Local and State Government and the Illinois Statehouse beat. We will be running this class like a newsroom as part of the Medill Illinois News Bureau (MINB: https://www.medill.northwestern.edu/journalism/graduate-journalism/exclusive-opportunities/medill-illinois-news-bureau.html) based in the Medill Chicago Newsroom. The course and the Bureau's work are a partnership with Capitol News Illinois (CNI: https://capitolnewsillinois.com/), which will be publishing many of the stories of the student fellows admitted to this class. Students must apply for select spots in this class by filing out the Medill Illinois News Bureau - Q2 Reporting Course Selective Application in October and getting accepted into the course in advance as MINB Statehouse Fellows. Students in the Politics, Policy & Foreign Affairs specialization will have the priority in Winter Quarter since they will be in Washington, D.C., Spring and Summer Quarters.

The course will prepare eight to ten admitted students to report on all aspects of local and state government, the State Legislature, and Illinois and national politics. Stories will range from breaking news and light enterprise to features, investigative and deeper dive stories covering the Illinois and Chicago news and policy beats. This includes state government officials and agencies, the Illinois General Assembly, the governor's office and the executive branch, and even some stories on the Illinois Supreme Court, as well as stories about Chicago's City Hall, Chicago Public Schools and Chicago news conferences with an Illinois focus. This class will include students in the Politics, Policy & Foreign Affairs specialization and also students from other MSJ specializations—and some of those latter students may want to apply again for the advanced reporting class on the Statehouse Beat in the Spring Quarter—if not admitted in Winter Quarter—that will continue using MINB Student Fellows to work on stories and beats with Capitol News Illinois.

Students will be required to travel to Springfield regularly when the legislature is in session, and students will be getting invaluable, on-the-ground experience reporting from the Illinois State Capitol. Each Statehouse Fellow will be taking three to four trips to Springfield during the quarter and other travels as appropriate for other stories around Illinois. This also means students admitted to this class should not schedule classes on Wednesdays and Thursdays in the Winter Quarter if possible (or try to work with instructors) to allow Tuesday-Thursday travel to Springfield on any given week. Students will explore reporting assignments with Medill's partner, Capitol News Illinois (CNI), and work through an innovative Medill bureau to place stories with CNI (https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/author/medill/). This course will include discussions, readings and some guest lectures and field trips, and the class will operate like a newsroom with news meetings and one-on-one editing sessions to prepare students to report for the Medill Illinois News Bureau. Statehouse Fellows with the Bureau started working in the Fall Quarter 2024 and worked through Winter, Spring and Summer Quarters in 2025 and 2026 publishing stories for CNI. For the first time, an undergraduate Junior Resident is serving as a Statehouse Fellow this Fall Quarter. Given the policies and conduct of the federal administration, students may cover aspects of local and state government and politics that intersect with that of the current administration and its policies, explaining local and state impacts of those policies.

American politics in the 21st Century have become increasingly divided, bitter and rancorous, culminating in the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection by a violent mob storming the U.S. Capitol and an attempt by members of Congress to undo the lawful result of the 2020 presidential election. Protests in Chicago and Milwaukee during the 2024 Democratic and Republican National Conventions underscored the divisions in the heartland and across the U.S. on issues ranging from immigration to the war in Gaza to the fights over abortion rights, healthcare, energy and education. The 2024 presidential campaign and the election of Donald Trump to a second term as president has set in motion controversial government policies and programs that will continue to reverberate through state and local government during Winter Quarter, and this course will provide excellent lessons in real time for discussion, brainstorming, and producing stories on state and local government and related national politics, how to cover them, and what reactions they prompt in the legislature and state government. The results of the Nov. 3 Midterm elections will have policy impacts and implications for Illinois programs and policies, providing a range of possible stories for our Statehouse Fellows.

Doreen Weisenhaus
Office Hours: After class and by appointment
course_details.Overview of class: A Chicago police officer fatally shoots a teenager, but police refuse to release dash-cam video until a journalist invokes the Illinois Freedom of Information Act. A lawsuit accusing the Chicago City Council of violating open meeting laws is filed after reporters learn of private discussions on the city's response to the Covid-19 pandemic. Journalists covering protests outside an ICE immigration facility file a federal lawsuit accusing police of violating their First Amendment rights for violently interfering with their news gathering, including spraying them with tear gas. As these and other cases demonstrate, journalists in these contentious times need to turn to the law to confront increasing challenges to newsgathering and investigative reporting. This unique joint Practicum with Northwestern's Pritzker School of Law - comprised of externships and weekly seminars - aims to advance the public's access to information, to hold institutions accountable, and to defend free speech and press freedom. Through externships of 10-12 hours a week at media organizations, non-profits, and press-advocacy groups (provided and matched by faculty), Medill students will learn how to research and prepare access requests and how to research legal or policy matters related to investigative and accountability issues. Through lectures and guest speakers, students will be introduced to the major transparency laws and other topics inherent in the relevant casework. Working collaboratively with law students, Medill students will deepen their understanding of the subject matters, share their experiences on outside projects, and discuss the legal and ethical issues that arise. Students will be matched with existing externships.

course_details.Overview of class: For over 2000 years, London has been a cultural and financial capital. Britain led the largest empire in world history, a quarter of the world's land mass. And now it votes to leave Europe! We will explore in a class what makes you a leader, an innovator, a communicator and a decision-maker that leads an organization, a team, a group of peers. We will use London as a means to consider your own capacity to grow and develop in five main ways: how to be the best at oral communication; how to develop and nurture the people who work for you and with you; how to develop and execute good business plans for media and innovation; how to ensure your lens includes financial and economic literacy; how to build your negotiating, decision-making and interviewing skills so you can even negotiate your own career well. All without exams! London, even with Brexit, is still a cultural and financial capital. Are you a confident global cultural and financial media citizen? This course encourages the innovative, executive and communicative capacity that you have within to be a future leader.

course_details.Overview of class: Media is changing faster than old playbooks can keep up. Newsrooms, startups and independent creators face the same test: build something people value, backed by strategies that earn audience loyalty and revenue. For journalism, the stakes are higher: without a sustainable model, news organizations cannot survive. In this course you will learn to do both by developing the skills to identify audience needs, turn them into viable ideas, design for engagement and build revenue models that fit today's media environment, all in service of an evidence-based plan for your own new media product.

course_details.Overview of class: Sport is a social institution no less than education, religion or the military, and outside of the United States is increasingly covered that way. The tension in that coverage stems from the fact that sport is the highest-earning product in the global entertainment industry, while at the same time the "right to play" is a basic human right, enshrined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. This course will focus on sports in an international context for students who wish to cover sports or study them. Topics will include a basic introduction to the definitions of ‘modern' sport and modern human rights; the global sports media rights market; the work of international sport governing bodies, from the IOC to the CAS; gender and sex issues, particularly regarding women, intersex and transexual athletes; the legacy of colonialism on sports, particularly in Africa and Asia; "sportswashing" and the role of the Arab Gulf states in sponsoring and hosting international sports events. We will pay particular attention to human rights issues surrounding the 2026 World Cup and the 2028 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles. Primary assignments are weekly reading response paper, a series of student-led debates, and a final paper or book review. There will be guest speakers from the US and around the world during the term, all of them visiting virtually. Students will be expected to lead discussion.

course_details.Overview of class: In this class, students will learn about how to deliver military reporting from the inside out. The class will examine the lives of people in uniform and their role in American society and U.S. national defense. We will study how journalists cover the United States military, war, national security institutions, veterans, and conﬂict abroad. Students will also study the structure and culture of the U.S. armed forces, the evolution of war correspondence, Pentagon reporting, ethics and military technology. The course combines historical case studies, practical reporting, class discussions, readings and guest lectures. Students are expected to put forth a sustained, full-time effort to excel. They will learn best practices on how to cover military personnel and installations while also developing a deeper understanding of the military culture and role in the United States.
course_details.Class Materials (Required):
Students will be required to read only one of the books below, their choice. They will also be asked to write a piece inspired by the book, whether it be a book review, a thematic piece, a profile of the author or a Q&A with the author.

The Fighters — C.J. Chivers (from $10.37 on Amazon)

The Generals — Thomas E. Ricks (from $14.13 on Amazon)

Thank You for Your Service — David Finkel (from $13.04 on Amazon)

Each book covers a different aspect of the course, so students will be able to choose the theme and the book that interests them most.

course_details.Overview of class: This two-quarter, faculty-led newsroom experience brings students together with a professional news outlet to collaborate on a real-world, data-driven investigation focused on issues of local public interest. Students learn how to use data throughout the investigative reporting process, from finding, collecting and cleaning datasets to analyzing information, identifying patterns, uncovering disparities and developing evidence-based findings. Working as part of an investigative newsroom team, students combine data skills with traditional reporting techniques, including public records requests, source development, interviews and verification. The experience emphasizes collaborative, hands-on investigative journalism, with the goal of contributing to a publishable investigation.
